items.stem: Which of the following best describes "global network"?
options: The idea that improvements in transport and communications have reduced the relative distance between places
A set of interconnected places (nodes) linked by flows such as trade, finance, data and transport
The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is consumed
A policy of minimising involvement in international affairs and trade
items.answer: A set of interconnected places (nodes) linked by flows such as trade, finance, data and transport
items.markingKey: B. "global network" is a set of interconnected places (nodes) linked by flows such as trade, finance, data and transport.

items.stem: Briefly explain why submarine cables are important to global networks.
items.answer: They carry almost all intercontinental data; their landing points and routes determine which places are well connected, and damage to cables can disconnect countries, e.g. Tonga after the 2022 eruption.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They carry almost all intercontinental data; their landing points and routes determine which places are well connected, and damage to cables can disconnect countries, e.g. Tonga after the 2022 eruption. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Time-space compression means places are physically closer together." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Physical distances are unchanged; it is the time and cost of interactions that have fallen.
items.markingKey: Physical distances are unchanged; it is the time and cost of interactions that have fallen. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The distance from London to New York is about 5,570 km. Calculate the journey time by a sailing ship (about 10 km/h average) and by a jet airliner (about 850 km/h), and the factor by which travel time has been reduced. Explain how this illustrates time-space compression.
items.answer: 557 h (23.2 days) vs 6.6 h; reduced by a factor of 85; places are effectively "closer" in time, increasing flows of people, goods and ideas.
items.markingKey: A1 557 h; A1 6.6 h; A1 factor 85; R1 time-space compression.

items.stem:
The table shows data for a sample of countries from World Bank data (site: GDP per capita (US$ thousand, PPP), employment in agriculture (%)).
A: 21.2, 46; B: 26.0, 50; C: 19.5, 51; D: 53.0, 17; E: 43.6, 37; F: 50.1, 16; G: 66.9, 11; H: 17.3, 54.
Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rs = 1 − 6Σd² / (n³ − n)) and state whether the relationship is significant at the 0.05 level (one-tailed test; critical value for n = 8: 0.643).
items.answer: Σd² = 164; rs = 1 − 6×164/(8³ − 8) = -0.952; a negative correlation that is significant at the 0.05 level.
items.markingKey: M1 ranking both variables (rank 1 = highest); M1 d² summed: Σd² = 164; A1 rs = -0.952; R1 |rs| >= 0.643 so reject the null hypothesis.

items.stem: Outline one argument for and one argument against the view that technology is the most important factor in increasing global interactions.
items.answer: Technology enables interactions, but political and economic decisions determine their scale and direction.
items.markingKey: For: containerisation, jets, internet. Against: trade liberalisation, political decisions and TNC strategies. [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The gap between people and places with good access to information and communication technology and those without"?
items.answer: digital divide
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of digital divide.

items.stem: Distinguish between places that are "switched off" and places that are "switched on".
items.answer: Switched-on places are well connected to global flows (London, Singapore); switched-off places have limited connection due to remoteness, poverty, conflict or policy (rural Chad, North Korea).
items.markingKey: Switched-on places are well connected to global flows (London, Singapore); switched-off places have limited connection due to remoteness, poverty, conflict or policy (rural Chad, North Korea). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how time-space compression has changed global interactions.
items.answer: Faster, cheaper transport (jets, container ships) and instant communications allow goods, people, capital and information to move rapidly, enabling global supply chains, financial markets, tourism and migration.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Faster, cheaper transport (jets, container ships) and instant communications allow goods, people, capital and information to move rapidly, enabling global supply chains, financial markets, tourism and migration. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between relative distance and absolute distance.
items.answer: Absolute distance is the physical distance between places in km; relative distance is measured in time, cost or effort and has fallen with transport and communications technology.
items.markingKey: Absolute distance is the physical distance between places in km; relative distance is measured in time, cost or effort and has fallen with transport and communications technology. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using examples, explain how improvements in transport have caused time-space compression.
items.answer: e.g. sailing ships (London-Sydney about 100 days in 1850), steamships (about 40 days by 1900), jet aircraft (about 22 hours today); container ships have cut freight costs dramatically.
items.markingKey: e.g. sailing ships (London-Sydney about 100 days in 1850), steamships (about 40 days by 1900), jet aircraft (about 22 hours today); container ships have cut freight costs dramatically.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "isolationism"?
options: A policy of minimising involvement in international affairs and trade
The gap between people and places with good access to information and communication technology and those without
The reduction in the time taken to move goods, people and information between places, making the world effectively "shrink" (David Harvey)
A group of countries that reduce trade barriers between themselves, such as the EU, ASEAN or AfCFTA
items.answer: A policy of minimising involvement in international affairs and trade
items.markingKey: A. "isolationism" is a policy of minimising involvement in international affairs and trade.

items.stem: Explain why landlocked states often have lower participation in global trade.
items.answer: They depend on neighbours' ports, roads and political goodwill; transit delays, extra border crossings and longer distances raise costs and reduce competitiveness.

items.stem: Shenzhen became China's first special economic zone in:
items.markingKey: A. It grew from about 30,000 people to over 17 million.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "global network".
items.answer: A set of interconnected places (nodes) linked by flows such as trade, finance, data and transport
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a set of interconnected places (nodes) linked by flows such as trade, finance, data and transport. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "carbon leakage".
items.answer: The shift of emissions-intensive production to countries with weaker climate policies
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the shift of emissions-intensive production to countries with weaker climate policies. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how a resource curse can reduce development.
items.answer: Commodity exports raise the exchange rate (Dutch disease) and harm other exports; revenues encourage corruption and rent-seeking; price volatility destabilises budgets; competition for resources can fuel conflict (e.g. DR Congo minerals).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Commodity exports raise the exchange rate (Dutch disease) and harm other exports; revenues encourage corruption and rent-seeking; price volatility destabilises budgets; competition for resources can fuel conflict (e.g. DR Congo minerals). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the world has not "shrunk" equally for all places.
items.answer: Connections are concentrated between global cities and well-connected regions; remote, poor and landlocked places have fewer flights, slower internet and higher costs, so relative distance remains large (the digital divide).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Connections are concentrated between global cities and well-connected regions; remote, poor and landlocked places have fewer flights, slower internet and higher costs, so relative distance remains large (the digital divide). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how global supply chains increase the carbon footprint of products.
items.answer: Components travel between many countries for processing and assembly, adding transport emissions; production is often in countries with coal-heavy electricity.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Components travel between many countries for processing and assembly, adding transport emissions; production is often in countries with coal-heavy electricity. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between physical factors affecting global participation and human factors affecting global participation.
items.answer: Physical factors include location, landlocked status, relief, climate and natural resources; human factors include political systems, policies, infrastructure, education and conflict.
items.markingKey: Physical factors include location, landlocked status, relief, climate and natural resources; human factors include political systems, policies, infrastructure, education and conflict. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Technology always reduces inequality between places." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It can widen gaps when well-connected places gain first and remote places are left behind.
items.markingKey: It can widen gaps when well-connected places gain first and remote places are left behind. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Buying local food always has the lowest carbon footprint." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Local food produced in heated greenhouses or with high inputs can have a larger footprint than imported food shipped by sea.
items.markingKey: Local food produced in heated greenhouses or with high inputs can have a larger footprint than imported food shipped by sea. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Between 1990 and 2002 the merchandise exports of a copper-exporting South American country changed from 155.3 to 133.8 US$ billion. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (133.8 − 155.3) ÷ 155.3 × 100; A1 -13.8% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem:
The data below were collected for a sample of countries from the KOF Swiss Economic Institute (site: KOF globalisation index, GDP per capita (US$ thousand, PPP)).
A: 44.0, 12.2; B: 88.6, 80.0; C: 54.7, 28.6; D: 58.6, 40.3; E: 65.0, 38.6; F: 87.3, 72.2; G: 73.3, 59.3; H: 74.0, 55.5.
Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rs = 1 − 6Σd² / (n³ − n)) and state whether the relationship is significant at the 0.05 level (one-tailed test; critical value for n = 8: 0.643).
items.answer: Σd² = 4; rs = 1 − 6×4/(8³ − 8) = 0.952; a positive correlation that is significant at the 0.05 level.
items.markingKey: M1 ranking both variables (rank 1 = highest); M1 d² summed: Σd² = 4; A1 rs = 0.952; R1 |rs| >= 0.643 so reject the null hypothesis.

items.stem: A firm moves 40 tonnes of goods from Mumbai to London (about 7,200 km). Emission factors: rail 25 g CO₂ per tonne-km; air freight 600 g CO₂ per tonne-km. Calculate the emissions (tonnes CO₂) for each mode and how many times higher the larger figure is.
items.answer: rail: 7.20 t; air freight: 172.80 t; ratio 24.0
items.markingKey: M1 tonnes × km × factor ÷ 10⁶; A1 7.20; A1 172.80; A1 ratio 24.0.

items.stem: "Global trade is the main cause of rising greenhouse gas emissions." To what extent do you agree with this statement? In your answer, consider the perspectives of people in high- and low-income countries.
items.answer: Trade contributes significantly, but domestic energy systems are the main cause.
items.markingKey: Paper 3 (b) indicative content - for: transport emissions from shipping and aviation; carbon leakage to coal-based economies. Against: most emissions come from domestic energy, buildings and land use; trade can spread efficient technologies such as solar panels. Judgement: Trade contributes significantly, but domestic energy systems are the main cause. items.stem: "Natural resource wealth is more of a curse than a blessing for development." To what extent do you agree with this statement? In your answer, consider the perspectives of people in high- and low-income countries.
